entries.title: Claude wrote machine-checked no-crash proofs for 239 OSS-Fuzz entry points across 123 libraries at the RISC-V binary level by turning fuzz harnesses into specs
entries.author: Keane Lucas et al. (Anthropic, Theorem)
entries.summary: Anthropic and Theorem had Claude prove, in Rocq, that 239 OSS-Fuzz entry points in 123 open-source libraries never crash (no memory-safety error or failed assertion) for any input up to 64 MB, after patching the bugs it found along the way. The spec is derived mechanically from the existing fuzz harness plus formal RISC-V and Linux-process semantics, so the ~180M lines of proof need no human review: trust reduces to the semantics, the theorem statements and the Rocq checker. Scope is narrow (single-threaded static RISC-V binaries, fixed memory budget) and compute is large, but it moves formal verification from niche to a pipeline step.

lessons.point: LLM-written formal proofs now scale to production libraries at the binary level, not just toy programs.
lessons.excerpt: proved that there are no crashes on any input (up to 64 MB) for 239 entry points across 123 different OSS-Fuzz libraries

lessons.point: The spec problem is sidestepped by reusing what developers already wrote: an existing fuzz harness becomes the property to prove.
lessons.excerpt: automatically converting their preexisting compilable test suites into a spec

lessons.point: Machine checking replaces review of the AI output: the trusted base is the semantics, the theorem statements and the checker, not the 600k-line proofs.
lessons.excerpt: virtually none of it needs to be manually reviewed

lessons.point: The guarantee is scoped: it holds only for single-threaded static RISC-V binaries on Linux under a memory budget, and bugs may remain in the trusted components.
lessons.excerpt: assume that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V CPU using Linux OS

lessons.point: Attempting proofs is itself a bug finder: failures pointed at real bugs that fuzzing had missed.
lessons.excerpt: the process of attempting to prove these specs discovered hundreds of bugs

entries.threat: AI-accelerated bug discovery and exploit chaining outpacing test-based assurance for memory-unsafe code.
entries.conditions: C/C++ libraries with existing fuzz harnesses; proofs currently limited to single-threaded static RISC-V Linux binaries.
entries.mitigations: Turn fuzz harnesses into no-crash specs and have an LLM produce checker-verified proofs; review the theorem statements and trusted semantics rather than proof text.
entries.takeaway: If you maintain C/C++ with fuzz harnesses, those harnesses are now candidate proof specs: an LLM plus a proof checker can turn 'fuzzed a lot' into 'proved no crash' for the covered scope.

actionable.title: Fuzz-harness-to-proof pipeline
actionable.detail: For a C/C++ library already in OSS-Fuzz, try Theorem's published add-project Claude skill and pipeline on one entry point; review only the generated theorem statement and assumptions, and treat proof failures as bug reports.

entries.prior_art: seL4 and CompCert (human-written verification at 10x code effort), binary-level verifiers like Alive2, LLM proof assistants (Baldur, AlphaProof), and AI bug finding (Big Sleep, AIxCC). None showed LLM-written, machine-checked binary-level proofs at this scale.
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier: all excerpts verbatim; novelty 78 vs 75 (kept 75); relevance 72; noted trusted components may hold bugs and the compute cost is large.

entries.title: Sentry's Next.js tunnelRoute skipped middleware for everything under the tunnel path, not just the requests its rewrite served (GHSA-mchm-gjx6-7h55)
entries.summary: @sentry/nextjs's tunnelRoute option forwards browser events through a path on your own Next.js server and tells the SDK to skip middleware for them. The skip matched every path under the tunnel prefix, while the rewrite only served the exact tunnel path with the o and p parameters, so any app route that resolves under that prefix (a direct collision or a root dynamic segment like app/[locale]) ran without middleware. It is only an authorization bypass where middleware is the sole authz layer; fixed in 9.47.2, 10.75.2 and 11.0.0-rc.1.

lessons.point: The bug is a scope mismatch: an exemption (skip middleware) was matched more broadly than the thing it existed to protect (the rewrite).
lessons.excerpt: The middleware skip was wider than the rewrite.

lessons.point: Requests in the gap reach application routes with middleware never executed.
lessons.excerpt: Requests in that gap go to your application instead of Sentry, and your middleware never runs on them.

lessons.point: It is only exploitable when middleware is the sole authorization layer for the colliding routes; server-side session checks still hold.
lessons.excerpt: your middleware is the only place that enforces authorization for those routes

lessons.point: The durable fix is defense in depth: enforce authorization in the route, layout or data-access layer as well as middleware.
lessons.excerpt: Enforce authorization in the route, layout or data-access path as well as in middleware.

lessons.point: Only webpack builds are affected.
lessons.excerpt: Turbopack builds are not affected

entries.threat: Unauthenticated access to Next.js routes whose only authorization check lives in middleware, by requesting them under the Sentry tunnel prefix.
entries.conditions: tunnelRoute set; webpack build; an app route resolving under the tunnel path (including a root dynamic segment); middleware-only authorization.
entries.mitigations: Upgrade @sentry/nextjs to 9.47.2 / 10.75.2 / 11.0.0-rc.1; move tunnelRoute to a path no route can resolve under; build with Turbopack; enforce authz in routes or data access, not only middleware.
entries.takeaway: Any SDK or framework that exempts paths from middleware is a potential authz bypass: if middleware is your only authorization check, grep your dependencies for middleware skips.

actionable.title: Audit middleware exemptions and add route-level authz
actionable.detail: Upgrade @sentry/nextjs; then list every matcher/skip that bypasses Next.js middleware (Sentry tunnel, static assets, health checks) and confirm each protected route also checks the session server-side in its layout, route handler or data-access layer.

entries.prior_art: Next.js CVE-2025-29927 (x-middleware-subrequest middleware bypass) established that middleware-only authorization in Next.js is fragile; this is a new, SDK-introduced instance of the same class.
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier: all excerpts verbatim; novelty 40 (same); stressed the route-collision precondition and that server-side session checks still protect routes.

editorial.reason: Critical GHSA in a ubiquitous Next.js SDK with a transferable lesson: middleware exemptions are authz bypasses wherever middleware is the only authorization check.

entries.title: 38.9% of agent-generated PRs carry a security smell - but humans introduce most of the real leaked secrets
entries.author: A H M Nazmus Sakib et al.
entries.summary: A large-scale study of the AIDev dataset classified security smells across 16,112 file changes in 4,022 agent-generated pull requests. 38.9% of agent PRs contain at least one security smell and supply-chain integrity issues make up 82.3% of them - but the counterintuitive result is that human collaborators introduce 67.6% of the genuine leaked secrets in these agent-assisted workflows, and review catches almost none of them. All percentages are downstream of an LLM-as-a-judge classification pipeline plus manual review, so treat the precision of the figures accordingly.

lessons.point: Supply-chain integrity dominates the detected smell taxonomy (82.3%); the abstract does not enumerate the remaining categories, so everything else combined is a small residual - point provenance and dependency controls at agent output.
lessons.excerpt: 38.9% of agent-generated PRs contain at least one security smell, with supply chain integrity issues accounting for 82.3% of all detected security smells

lessons.point: Blaming the agent misreads the data: humans introduced most genuine leaked secrets, which the authors describe only as suggesting a *potential* reduction in developer vigilance - an association, not a causal finding.
lessons.excerpt: human collaborators are responsible for introducing 67.6% of genuine leaked secrets within these agent-assisted workflows

lessons.point: Existing review is not a control here - automated and human review together missed 81.1% of these credentials before integration.
lessons.excerpt: existing automated and human review processes fail to detect 81.1% of these credentials prior to integration

entries.threat: Security debt accumulates in high-impact file paths faster than human review capacity, with hard-coded credentials making up 99.6% of critical-severity smells.
entries.conditions: Repositories that accept autonomous coding-agent pull requests through a conventional human review process.
entries.mitigations: Enforce secret scanning as a merge gate rather than a review step; apply provenance/dependency-integrity checks to agent PRs; add context-aware guardrails at the human-AI collaboration point rather than at final review.
entries.takeaway: Gate agent PRs with automated secret and dependency-integrity checks - human review demonstrably does not catch this class, and the humans are introducing most of it.
entries.prior_art: That LLM-generated code contains vulnerabilities is well documented (Copilot-era studies onward). The delta is scale and attribution on real agent PRs - the 67.6% human-origin secrets finding inverts the 'the agent is the risk' framing. Methodologically it applies an existing technique (LLM-as-judge + manual coding) to a new dataset rather than introducing a new method. Accepted at the KDD 2026 AgenticSE workshop.
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier: removed invented contrast categories (injection/logic bugs); restored the authors' 'potential' hedge on developer vigilance; surfaced that all figures come from an LLM-as-a-judge pipeline; novelty 68->57.

editorial.reason: Large-scale, widely-discussed finding on coding-agent risk with a concrete gate: automated secret + dependency-integrity scanning on agent PRs, because human review misses 81%.

entries.title: How we found 24 Android vulnerabilities using our open source AI security agent
entries.summary: GitHub Security Lab extended its open-source Taskflow Agent with Android-specific audit steps. One taskflow separates mobile from non-mobile entry points, and another checks a fixed list of vulnerability classes against each entry point. Together they found 24 vulnerabilities, including OsmAnd location tracking and a WebView account-takeover chain. The post is candid that LLMs over-report low-severity bugs, misjudge severity, and need PoC runs plus expert review.

lessons.point: Give the model a per-entry-point checklist of vulnerability classes so non-determinism doesn't skip the essential bug classes on less familiar platforms like Android.
lessons.excerpt: Since mobile application vulnerabilities are less widely known and LLMs are non-deterministic, we should ensure the LLM checks for certain essential vulnerabilities classes.

lessons.point: Run a strict checklist prompt several times alongside a broad open-ended prompt: the first catches the obvious bugs and the second finds the creative ones.
lessons.excerpt: By combining both prompts across multiple runs, we get the best of each

lessons.point: LLM auditors over-report low-impact or unrealistic-state bugs, even when told not to, so every finding needs expert triage.
lessons.excerpt: it often reported low-severity vulnerabilities, even when specifically told not to do so

lessons.point: Making the model write a proof of concept surfaces mitigating factors it otherwise misses; a debugger is the stronger fix for the false positives that remain.
lessons.excerpt: the only way to fix these issue is to give the LLM a debugger to run the proof of concept and original code

entries.takeaway: Scaffolded, platform-specific taskflows make LLMs effective Android bug hunters, but severity and exploitability still need a PoC and a human.

actionable.title: Two-stage Android audit: classify entry points, then checklist per entry point
actionable.detail: Stage 1: enumerate exported activities, services, receivers, deeplinks and JS bridges, and separate mobile from non-mobile entry points. Stage 2: for each entry point, prompt for its class-specific checklist (intents: confused deputy, insecure broadcast; WebView: XSS, exposed bridges; files: path traversal). Run that strict pass several times plus one open-ended pass, then require a PoC for every finding before human triage.

entries.prior_art: Earlier GHSL Taskflow Agent posts on generic audit taskflows, and LLM-assisted SAST triage; the delta is the Android-specific entry-point and checklist decomposition plus its field results.
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier: all lessons supported; novelty 45 (vs 50), relevance 80.

editorial.reason: 24 real, disclosed Android vulnerabilities (OsmAnd location tracking, a WebView account-takeover chain) found with an open-source agent you can run today, plus candid lessons on LLM severity misjudgment and false positives.

entries.title: Next.js App Router: unauthenticated RCE in `use cache` functions that return multiple typed arrays (GHSA-673q-mjm6-r5xr)
entries.summary: A critical GHSA for npm/next reports that apps using the App Router with Cache Components can be driven to remote code execution when a `use cache` function returns multiple typed arrays, with no known workaround short of upgrading. The fetched advisory page captured only the CVSS boilerplate, so the details here come from the GHSA feed summary alone.

lessons.point: The vulnerable surface is the cache serialization path for typed arrays in App Router Cache Components.
lessons.excerpt: The application needs to have a `use cache` function that returns multiple typed arrays.

lessons.point: There is no configuration workaround; affected apps must upgrade.
lessons.excerpt: There is no known workaround for affected applications

entries.takeaway: Upgrade Next.js now if any `use cache` function returns typed arrays; there is no workaround.

actionable.title: Find `use cache` functions returning typed arrays
actionable.detail: Grep for 'use cache' in App Router code, check return values for Uint8Array/Float32Array etc., and upgrade Next.js to the patched release.

entries.prior_art: React Server Components serialization RCE (React2Shell, CVE-2025-55182) is the closest prior class: framework-level serialization of server data leading to RCE.

entries.title: Datadog's pathrunner automates 80+ AWS IAM privilege-escalation paths and hands defenders the CloudTrail events each run should have produced
entries.author: Seth Art
entries.summary: Datadog released pathrunner, a modular Metasploit-style framework that exploits the AWS IAM privilege-escalation paths catalogued in pathfinding.cloud, with identity import/switching, multiple payloads per module, managed 'attacker' infrastructure and a workspace report. The report lists the resources created and the CloudTrail events pathrunner expects to have triggered, turning a red-team run into a detection-engineering checklist. It is incremental over Pacu and Stratus Red Team; its value is the per-payload detection coverage it enables.

lessons.point: In cloud environments lateral movement is mostly identity-to-identity via credentials, so model attack paths as IAM graphs, not network hops.
lessons.excerpt: more often than not, penetration testers and real attacks are hopping from one cloud identity to another by accessing credentials

lessons.point: The tool ships a broad catalogue of exploit modules mapped to required permissions.
lessons.excerpt: As of October 2026, there are over 80 exploit modules in pathrunner.

lessons.point: Write detections per payload, not per single post-exploitation action: a detection for 'create admin user' is blind when the attacker picks another payload.
lessons.excerpt: if you walk through each and every pathrunner payload in your environment and build detections for each of them, you will have a much greater chance of catching malicious activity

lessons.point: The workspace report gives the blue team the CloudTrail events the run is expected to generate (Datadog's expectation, not a verified log) to check detections against.
lessons.excerpt: the report includes a table that lists all of the CloudTrail events that we think pathrunner would have triggered

lessons.point: Demonstrated exploitability is the triage signal for misconfigurations, as a public PoC is for CVEs.
lessons.excerpt: An offensive tool demonstrates the impact of an attack, enabling defenders to prioritize exploitable misconfigurations based on how impactful they are.

entries.takeaway: Run pathrunner in a sandbox (Pathfinding Labs) and use its CloudTrail report to test that every payload, not just one, trips a detection.

actionable.title: Detection coverage drill with pathrunner
actionable.detail: Deploy Pathfinding Labs in a sandbox account, run each pathrunner module with every payload, export `workspace report`, and diff the expected CloudTrail events against what your SIEM alerted on; file a detection gap per miss.

entries.prior_art: Pacu, Rhino Security's AWS escalation methods/CloudGoat, Stratus Red Team (per-technique detection testing), and Datadog's own pathfinding.cloud and Pathfinding Labs.
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier: all excerpts verbatim; novelty 40->35 (incremental over Pacu/Stratus); CloudTrail table is expected, not verified, events.

entries.title: Next.js Image Optimization API: unauthenticated RCE via SVG through an upstream sharp memory bug on glibc Linux (GHSA-2464-fhr4-w9xw)
entries.summary: A critical GHSA for npm/next reports that a memory-related bug in an upstream library used by Next.js Image Optimization can lead to remote code execution when SVG files are processed on glibc-based Linux; the workaround is to ensure the sharp version Next.js uses is new enough. The fetched advisory page captured only the CVSS boilerplate, so the details here come from the GHSA feed summary alone.

lessons.point: Server-side image optimization turns an image-library memory bug into unauthenticated RCE on the web tier.
lessons.excerpt: A memory-related vulnerability has been discovered in an upstream library used for Image Optimization can lead to possible remote code execution (RCE) when Next.js runs on glibc-based Linux.

lessons.point: The fix is a transitive dependency bump: pin a patched sharp.
lessons.excerpt: Ensure the version of `sharp` used by Next.js is greater

entries.takeaway: Pin a patched sharp under Next.js and consider disabling SVG optimization; image pipelines are unauthenticated RCE surface.

actionable.title: Check the sharp version Next.js resolves
actionable.detail: Run npm ls sharp in each Next.js app, upgrade to the patched sharp, and keep dangerouslyAllowSVG off unless required.

entries.prior_art: Astro's default image optimizer RCE via a libheif bug in sharp (GHSA-26w7-cxv4-gfx2), already in the story ledger: same class, different framework and codec.
entries.verify_note: Advisory body not captured (fetched page holds only CVSS boilerplate); lessons rest on the GHSA feed summary.

entries.title: A few notes on AWS Nitro Enclaves: KMS integration
entries.summary: Trail of Bits enumerates passive and active attack classes against the Nitro Enclave to AWS KMS communication channel: encryption-context omission, CMK substitution, attestation-request replay, and the fact that TLS to KMS terminates outside the HSM. They also flag an end-to-end verifiability gap: even with immutable key policies, AWS Support can restore default policies for a key owner, so there is no Certificate-Transparency-style public log a third-party client can independently verify.
entries.takeaway: Enclave-to-KMS attestation only closes the gap if you also hardcode the CMK ARN, attest the IAM role, and initiate TLS from inside the enclave; without that, active-attacker equivalence returns.

lessons.point: Attestation documents are not cryptographically bound to KMS requests, so a captured attestation is replayable for five minutes against any supported operation with attacker-chosen parameters.
lessons.excerpt: As attestations are not cryptographically bound to the requests, the attacker can use the attestation with any supported operation with arbitrary params.

lessons.point: KMS terminates TLS outside the HSM, so end-to-end confidentiality between the enclave and the HSM is not achievable and AWS insiders belong in the threat model.
lessons.excerpt: KMS terminates TLS outside of HSM ([most likely](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/cryptographic-details/internal-communication-security.html)), and the attestation's pubkey encryption is probably done outside of HSM. This makes it impossible to have an end-to-end TLS channel between enclave and HSM, and AWS insiders may theoretically constitute an active attacker threat.

lessons.point: Even immutable key policies do not deliver true end-to-end verifiability, because AWS Support can restore a default policy on the owner's request and there is no public append-only log a third party can audit.
lessons.excerpt: Note that key owners can always [contact AWS support to restore default key policies]... However, we are not aware of any "Certificate Transparency"-style public, append-only log for KMS key policies that an external party can independently verify.

lessons.point: The official aws-nitro-enclaves-sdk-c is C code that Trail of Bits found host-exploitable and recommends avoiding in favor of a Rust NSM library plus Boto3 for KMS.
lessons.excerpt: Amazon ships a lot of SDKs for various tasks. Among them is [`aws-nitro-enclaves-sdk-c`](https://github.com/aws/aws-nitro-enclaves-sdk-c) that provides tools and a library for enclaves-KMS communication. Avoid it: this particular SDK is written in C, and we found it contains vulnerabilities that can be used to exploit enclaves from the parent host.

actionable.title: Enclave-KMS hardening checklist
actionable.detail: For any enclave-KMS integration: hardcode CMK ARN (attested), attest the IAM role via sts:GetCallerIdentity, initiate TLS from inside the enclave with a pinned Amazon CA, use encryption contexts that the host cannot fully control, and monitor kms:PutKeyPolicy externally since AWS Support can restore default policies.

entries.prior_art: No direct pool entry; the Trail of Bits Nitro Enclaves attack-surface post is cited in this piece but not indexed. Standing claims do not cover KMS-enclave attestation replay.
entries.threat: A privileged host or malicious insider between enclave and KMS can swap ciphertexts, substitute CMKs, replay attestations, or bypass immutable key policies via AWS Support restoration.
entries.conditions: Applies when a Nitro Enclave uses KMS with attestation-based key access, does not initiate its own TLS to KMS, or uses key aliases instead of full CMK ARNs.
entries.mitigations: Bundle KMS CA cert inside the enclave and pin it; initiate TLS from within the enclave; attest full CMK ARN and IAM role; use encryption contexts under enclave control; deny kms:PutKeyPolicy globally; alarm on key deletion; publish a client-visible policy monitor. Prefer aws-nitro-enclaves-nsm-api (Rust) + Boto3 over aws-nitro-enclaves-sdk-c (C).
entries.verify_note: All four excerpts verified verbatim against raw_path. Cluster set to null because the piece is enclave-crypto/appsec and does not intersect the 13 clusters (nearest fit I is 'Deployment infra and sandboxing', but the material is HSM/KMS cryptography, not agent/LLM runtime).

entries.title: CISA KEV: Plex Media Server encoded-URI-scheme flaw CVE-2026-96654 exploited in the wild, part of a four-CVE chain
entries.summary: CISA added CVE-2026-96654, an improper neutralization of encoded URI schemes in Plex Media Server's web page, to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 20, 2026 with a three-day due date. Per the KEV entry it lets an attacker call other plugins' functions with their own parameters and chains with CVE-2026-96652, -96655 and -96656; NVD references a public 'plex2shell' write-up. The captured NVD page carries little technical detail, so this is a patch-now signal rather than a teachable root cause.

lessons.point: The flaw is confirmed exploited in the wild and listed in KEV, so self-hosted Plex servers should be patched now rather than on a normal cycle.
lessons.excerpt: This CVE is in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog

lessons.point: NVD links a third-party write-up titled plex2shell, indicating a public path from this chain to a shell.
lessons.excerpt: https://zmain.info/blog/plex2shell

entries.threat: Chained Plex Media Server bugs leading to plugin function invocation and arbitrary file write, exploited in the wild.
entries.conditions: Internet-reachable or LAN-exposed Plex Media Server on an unpatched version.
entries.mitigations: Apply the Plex Media Server update referenced in the vendor release notes; restrict exposure of the Plex web interface.
entries.takeaway: Patch Plex Media Server now: four chained CVEs are in KEV with a public plex2shell write-up.

actionable.title: Patch and inventory Plex servers
actionable.detail: Find Plex Media Server instances (including homelab hosts on corporate networks), update to the fixed release, and check whether the web interface is exposed to the internet.

entries.title: America bans imported robots due to supply chain and security risks
entries.summary: The FCC added foreign-made advanced robotic devices to the Covered List, effectively banning their import due to supply-chain and security risks. The National Security Determination frames networked robots as broad attack surfaces vulnerable to remote takeover, data exfiltration, and insecure OTA updates, and points to UniPwn on Unitree humanoids as a concrete example.
entries.takeaway: US regulators are treating networked physical robots as a critical-infrastructure supply-chain risk category on par with telecom gear.

lessons.point: US regulators now classify connected robots as broad attack surfaces subject to remote takeover, exfiltration, and OTA-update risk.
lessons.excerpt: modern bots are now constantly connected to networks “which creates broad attack surfaces and leaves them vulnerable to data exfiltration, remote disruption of the physical robot, and dependencies on unsecure over the air updates.”

lessons.point: The UniPwn flaws in Unitree humanoids are cited by name as the exemplar vulnerability motivating the ban.
lessons.excerpt: One example of those vulnerabilities mentioned in the document is the UniPwn flaws that made it possible for attackers to take over humanoid robots made by Chinese company Unitree.

lessons.point: The mechanism is import ban via the FCC Covered List, with a narrow Department of War carve-out and a country-of-manufacture (not country-of-ownership) exemption.
lessons.excerpt: the FCC decided the foreign-made advanced robotic devices belong on its Covered List of products for which imports are banned because they pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States and its residents.

actionable.title: Track FCC Covered List entries as a supply-chain admission signal beyond telecom
actionable.detail: Product-security teams that already gate procurement against the FCC Covered List for telecom should now extend that gate to robotics and other networked physical devices; the same list is being repurposed as a general-purpose national-security exclusion mechanism.

entries.prior_art: Prior FCC Covered List additions targeted Huawei/ZTE telecom gear and DJI drones; extending the same mechanism to humanoid robots is a category expansion of an established tool, not a novel regulatory technique.
entries.threat: Networked robots operating inside critical facilities can be remotely disrupted or exfiltrated via compromised firmware, OTA-update infrastructure, or embedded backdoors from the manufacturer's supply chain.
entries.conditions: Applies to future imports of foreign-made advanced robotic devices; already-approved models and stock, plus foreign-owned firms that manufacture in the US (e.g., Boston Dynamics), are exempt.
entries.mitigations: Import ban via FCC Covered List; case-by-case Department of War vouching for individual devices.
entries.verify_note: All three excerpts appear verbatim in raw file lines 126, 130, 136. Cluster set to null because this is policy/regulation news, explicitly listed as adjacent (news-lane only) in data/interests.yaml.

entries.prior_art: Many prior Pillow decompression-bomb and parser-hang DoS advisories; the inherited-method/overridden-tell() root cause is a routine variation.
entries.title: Pillow DoS: a 5.6 KB MIC file hangs n_frames at 100% CPU (GHSA-22hg-r758-rrw9)
entries.summary: A crafted 5.6 KB Microsoft Image Composer file makes Pillow loop forever at 100% CPU when code reads im.n_frames, on installs with the optional olefile package. MicImageFile overrides seek() and tell() but inherits TiffImageFile.n_frames, which relies on tell() advancing, so it re-parses the same directory endlessly. The hang raises no exception and grows no memory; the regression dates to Pillow 7.2.0 (2020).

lessons.point: Exposure depends on an optional dependency: only installs with olefile register the MIC plugin.
lessons.excerpt: This only affects installations that have the optional `olefile` package.

lessons.point: Root cause is a subclass that overrides the primitives an inherited method depends on; audit inherited methods when you change seek/tell semantics.
lessons.excerpt: It does not override the `n_frames` property, so the inherited TIFF implementation runs

lessons.point: Silent CPU hangs evade exception handlers and memory limits; untrusted parsing needs a wall-clock watchdog.
lessons.excerpt: The call never returns, raises no exception, and does not grow memory, so only an external watchdog stops it.

lessons.point: The bug has shipped since Pillow 7.2.0.
lessons.excerpt: first released in 7.2.0

entries.takeaway: Affects installs with olefile, back to Pillow 7.2.0. Parse untrusted images under a timeout and restrict Image.open to the formats you expect.

actionable.title: Bound untrusted image parsing
actionable.detail: Pass an explicit formats= allowlist to Image.open for user uploads, drop olefile if you don't need MIC/FPX, and run frame-count and re-save operations in a worker with a wall-clock timeout.

entries.threat: Denial of service: one crafted upload pins a worker at 100% CPU indefinitely.
entries.conditions: olefile installed; the application opens an untrusted image and reads n_frames (e.g. is-animated checks, save_all re-saves).
entries.mitigations: Upgrade Pillow when patched; restrict formats; remove olefile; enforce worker timeouts.

editorial.reason: Fresh HIGH advisory in Pillow, which nearly every Python upload path uses; the fix pattern (formats allowlist, drop olefile, wall-clock timeouts) applies today.

entries.title: raml-kql: one KQL query across many Log Analytics workspaces and Entra tenants without a Defender multi-tenant org
entries.author: Luca Ramseyer
entries.summary: Raml KQL is an open-source VS Code-style desktop app that fans one KQL query out to many Azure Log Analytics/Sentinel workspaces across Entra tenants and accounts (found via Lighthouse delegations and guest access) and merges the results with tenant and workspace on every row. It runs with the analyst's delegated permissions and no stored secrets, aliases customer names on screen and keeps a hash-chained audit log. A convenience tool for MSSPs and consultants without a Defender MTO, not a new capability.

lessons.point: Cross-tenant hunting without a Defender MTO is possible from the analyst's own delegated access.
lessons.excerpt: Run one KQL query against many Azure Log Analytics workspaces at once, across many Entra tenants and many signed-in accounts

lessons.point: The design keeps no credentials of its own: it acts only with the user's delegated permissions.
lessons.excerpt: Raml KQL only ever does what you are allowed to do: it uses your delegated permissions and holds no secrets or service principals.

lessons.point: It records query provenance without storing customer data.
lessons.excerpt: A hash-chained audit log records what ran where, without result values.

entries.title: Trail of Bits Runs an Independent, From-Scratch Auditor for Signal's Key Transparency System
entries.summary: Signal's Automatic Key Verification depends on independent auditors maintaining consistency of a global public-key map; Trail of Bits operates one of the three required auditors (alongside Signal and Cloudflare), implemented from scratch (not from Signal's reference implementation) for independent verification. Clients require signatures from all three auditors within the last seven days, so a fully malicious Signal server can maintain a split view of the key map for at most one week before client warnings appear.
entries.takeaway: Signal's key transparency is bounded by its auditor-signature freshness window: a malicious server can show different keys to different users for up to a week before detection.

lessons.point: Clients currently require valid signatures from three independently-operated auditors (Signal, Cloudflare, and Trail of Bits), not just one, to accept a given key-map state.
lessons.excerpt: Clients currently require signatures from each of three auditors: one operated by Signal, one operated by Cloudflare, and one operated by Trail of Bits.

lessons.point: Auditor signatures must be within the last seven days, so a fully malicious server could maintain a split view of the public-key map for up to a week before clients start warning users.
lessons.excerpt: within the last seven days. If the server does not present valid auditor signatures, the client will raise a warning and Automatic Key Verification will fail. A fully malicious server may therefore maintain a split view of the system for at most one week before client applications start to display warning messages.

lessons.point: Trail of Bits deliberately implemented its auditor from scratch based on the published specification, rather than reusing Signal's own reference implementation, specifically to provide genuinely independent verification rather than validating the same code against itself.

actionable.title: Quantify the detection-latency window of any key-transparency or trust-log design you evaluate
actionable.detail: When evaluating a key-transparency or certificate-transparency-style system, explicitly quantify the maximum time a malicious operator could maintain an undetected split view before an auditor-freshness requirement triggers a client warning — for Signal's Automatic Key Verification, that bound is one week.
